slides.title:
Frozen models.
Better retrieval?
slides.subtitle: Test-time retrieval with black-box reranker feedback and no model weight updates.
slides.takeaway: Can better feedback change where we search?

notes.text: Our project asks whether a deployed retrieval system can improve at test time while both model backbones remain frozen.
notes.exactLocation: BRIEF: User brief, 16 Nov 2026: Queos Labs IRE presentation; no encoder or reranker weight updates; source-backed script and proposed complementary-feedback study.

notes.text: We assume that the embedding service returns vectors and that a reranker returns relevance scores for selected query-document pairs.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: Appendix §8, PDF p.13, final paragraph on the returned-embedding and downstream-search interfaces; §2.1, p.3, opening setup paragraph.

notes.text: The editable object is an external query representation, so the method still learns even though it does not fine-tune either model.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: Figure 1, PDF p.2, caption; TTT-M: §2.2, pp.3–4, Eqs.3–4, the residual is the optimization variable.

notes.text: We will follow the progression from TOUR to ReFIT and then to the reusable state in TTT-Embed.
notes.exactLocation: BRIEF: User brief, 16 Nov 2026: Queos Labs IRE presentation; no encoder or reranker weight updates; source-backed script and proposed complementary-feedback study.

notes.text: After the papers, we will inspect our SCIDOCS reproduction gap and the reported FiQA task-wise TTT pilot.
notes.exactLocation: RUN and RUN-CI: completed SCIDOCS report and bootstrap interval. FIQA_RUN: working report §4, FiQA task-wise TTT-Embed row; this is a reported project pilot, not independently recomputed evidence.

notes.text: Finally, can candidates covering complementary evidence teach a better residual under the same feedback budget?
notes.exactLocation: HYPOTHESIS: SOURCE_LEDGER.md, Hypothesis boundary. Coverage-aware selection may improve residual learning at fixed teacher budget. This combination is proposed here, not established by DISCo, TTT-Embed or our completed runs.

notes.text: That last step is the hypothesis we want to test, rather than a result we can already claim.
notes.exactLocation: HYPOTHESIS: SOURCE_LEDGER.md, Hypothesis boundary. Coverage-aware selection may improve residual learning at fixed teacher budget. This combination is proposed here, not established by DISCo, TTT-Embed or our completed runs.

slides.title:
What should expensive
feedback buy us?
slides.subtitle: The Microsoft research challenge is the starting point.
slides.takeaway: We narrow the problem to useful adaptation after deployment.

notes.text: The Microsoft challenge asks how high-quality reward feedback can improve retrieval models and downstream retrieval or generation.
notes.exactLocation: MSR: supplied challenge text, Summary, sole paragraph.

notes.text: It identifies three practical questions: which query-document pairs deserve scoring, which learning loss should use those scores, and how to control computational cost.
notes.exactLocation: MSR: Description, research questions (1) Data Selection, (2) Loss Formulation, and (3) Computational Efficiency.

notes.text: These decisions are connected: a powerful teacher helps only when we spend its judgments well.
notes.exactLocation: MSR: our synthesis of research questions (1)–(3), not a separately reported paper finding.

notes.text: Our project narrows that broad post-training agenda to a deployed system with frozen model weights and a fixed document index.
notes.exactLocation: BRIEF: user-requested no-weight-update setting. TTT-I: §2 opening paragraph, PDF p.3, fixed backbone and index.

notes.text: The question becomes what can be learned outside those models, directly from the feedback available at inference.
notes.exactLocation: BRIEF: our problem formulation. TTT-I: Introduction, paragraph on learning an external vector from returned embeddings.

notes.text: The literature supplies several query-update mechanisms, while our proposed study returns to the first Microsoft question: which documents should receive expensive feedback?
notes.exactLocation: MSR: question (1), Data Selection. HYPOTHESIS: our candidate-selection proposal; the Microsoft challenge does not name it.

notes.text: This is our scoped research problem, not a method prescribed by Microsoft.
notes.exactLocation: BRIEF: User brief, 16 Nov 2026: Queos Labs IRE presentation; no encoder or reranker weight updates; source-backed script and proposed complementary-feedback study.

pointers: Move across “Select → Learn → Spend”.
End on the selection column; it returns near the end of the talk.

slides.title:
What can we change
at inference?
slides.subtitle: Black box means an output interface is available; internal weights and gradients are not required.
slides.takeaway: Frozen encoders. Frozen reranker. Editable vector.

notes.text: There are three interfaces in our setting: an embedding service, a document-vector index, and a relevance-scoring teacher.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: §2.1, PDF p.3, opening paragraph; Appendix §8, PDF p.13, final access-assumptions paragraph.

notes.text: We can read their outputs and issue another vector search, but we do not update encoder weights, reranker weights, or stored document embeddings.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: Figure 1 caption, PDF p.2; §2 opening paragraph, p.3. TTT-M: §2.2 Eq.4 optimizes only the external residual.

notes.text: Instead, we optimize a small vector after the embedding service has produced its answer.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-M: §2.2, PDF pp.3–4, Eq.3 (vector addition) and Eq.4 (residual objective).

notes.text: An inaccessible retriever cannot be fine-tuned through a vector-only interface.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: Introduction paragraph on parameter access; Appendix §8 final paragraph. Claim is restricted to a vector-only API, not all services called black boxes.

notes.text: A black-box reranker by itself does not prevent training an accessible retriever, because its scores can still supply targets.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: Source ledger, output-interface reasoning. This follows from scores being usable targets when a separate retriever is trainable; it is a clarification, not an experiment.

notes.text: Our restriction is therefore no model weight updates, with output access sufficient for external optimization.
notes.exactLocation: BRIEF: user-requested frozen-model scope. TTT-I: Appendix §8 final paragraph, output access and control of vector search.

notes.text: If a service returns only document identifiers and offers no vector interface, this assumption may fail.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: Appendix §8, PDF p.13, final paragraph distinguishing the returned-vector setting from a service exposing only ranked identifiers.

notes.text: Keep that boundary in mind when applying the method to closed models.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: Appendix §8 final paragraph; explanatory reminder of the stated interface boundary.

pointers: Point to the two locked model boxes, then the blue external vector.
Read the allowed interface row; do not say that the teacher is unavailable.

slides.title:
Why is reranking
not enough?
slides.subtitle: A stronger judge can only reorder the candidates it receives.
slides.takeaway: A missed document needs another retrieval step.

notes.text: A dense retriever quickly searches precomputed document vectors and returns a short candidate list.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-I: §3.1, PDF p.2, paragraph after Eq.3 on precomputed passage embeddings and nearest-neighbor retrieval.

notes.text: A cross-encoder reranker reads each query-document pair jointly and assigns a more detailed relevance score.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-I: §3.1, PDF p.3, reranker paragraph before Eq.4; Introduction, paragraph comparing dual and cross encoders.

notes.text: In the diagram, the relevant document outside the candidate boundary never reaches that judge.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: original candidate-set schematic. The unseen relevant item is an illustrative example, not a retrieved case from the papers.

notes.text: Reordering a fixed set of K documents can improve their order, but cannot change Recall at K for that same set.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-I: Abstract ¶1 and Introduction opening paragraph. Fixed-set cardinality qualifier makes the Recall@K claim precise.

notes.text: Reranking 125 documents and keeping 100 can improve Recall at 100, making it a useful comparator.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §4.2, PDF pp.3–4, final comparison-design paragraph: retrieve/rerank125 but evaluate Recall@100.

notes.text: The feedback question is whether the scores can change the query vector and send it back into the full index.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-I: Figure 1 and Introduction paragraph describing inference-time distillation followed by second retrieval.

notes.text: That second search could retrieve an item absent from the first list, rather than only reshuffling documents already seen.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-I: Figure 1 caption and Introduction distillation paragraph; possibility of discovery is not a per-query guarantee.

notes.text: The next methods turn this possibility into an optimization procedure.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: Sung et al., Findings ACL 2023. PDF pp.3–5, §§3.1–3.5; Eqs.7–13. Encoders fixed: §3.1 ¶1. One step then retrieval: §3.2 paragraph after Eq.10. Caching: §3.5.; REFIT-M: PDF p.3, §3.2 Eqs.5–7 and Algorithm 1; §4.1 (separate min-max normalization, teacher T=2, n=100, learning rate .005); §4.2 (rerank 125 comparator).

pointers: Point to the outlined candidate set, then the single relevant item outside it.
Trace the second-search arrow back into the full corpus.

slides.title:
Ask. Move.
Search again.
slides.subtitle: TOUR optimizes the already-computed query representation.
slides.takeaway: The index stays fixed while the query moves.

notes.text: Start at the original query vector, q zero, and retrieve nearby candidates from the fixed index.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.1, PDF p.3, first two paragraphs; Eq.7 scores the retrieved candidates.

notes.text: TOUR asks a cross-encoder to score those candidates and treats the outputs as pseudo relevance feedback.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.1, PDF p.3, Eq.7 and following paragraph on pseudo labels without gold relevance.

notes.text: The query representation then takes a gradient step using that signal, while both encoders remain fixed.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.1 opening paragraph (fixed encoders); §3.2, PDF p.4, Eq.10 (query-vector gradient descent).

notes.text: Follow the blue arrow to q one: fresh retrieval can now return a different neighborhood.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.2, PDF p.4, paragraph after Eq.10 (one step followed by retrieval); Figure 1 (schematic vector movement).

notes.text: The method can repeat this retrieve-score-update process, with cached scores and early stopping reducing some repeated work.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.5, PDF p.5, sole paragraph on maximum iterations, early stopping and cached reranker scores.

notes.text: The number of rounds is task-dependent: its reported settings allow up to three for phrase question answering and one for passage retrieval.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: Appendix D, PDF p.14, Table 7, Max iterations row: 3 for phrase QA and 1 for both passage settings.

notes.text: The mechanism is moving the query and searching again; TOUR does not always run three rounds.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.2 Eq.10 and following paragraph. TOUR-R: Appendix D Table 7; task-specific interpretation.

notes.text: Next, we examine how TOUR converts teacher scores into a learning signal.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-HS: §3.2 and §3.3 headings and objectives; presentation transition.

pointers: Trace the loop clockwise: retrieve, score, update, retrieve.
Point to moving q₀ and q₁; the gray document points never move.

slides.title:
Hard labels,
or soft guidance?
slides.subtitle: Both are pseudo feedback. The distinction belongs to TOUR.
slides.takeaway: Hard selects a set. Soft preserves relative preferences.

notes.text: TOUR provides the hard and soft feedback objectives; these are not ReFIT variants.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-HS: §3.2 TOUR with Hard Labels and §3.3 TOUR with Soft Labels; ReFIT §2 acknowledges these as TOUR variants.

notes.text: In the hard version, teacher probabilities select a small pseudo-positive set using a cumulative-probability threshold.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-HS: §3.2, PDF pp.3–4, Eq.8 and adjacent paragraph specifying a smallest cumulative-probability pseudo-positive set.

notes.text: The hard loss increases total student probability on that set, without requiring it to copy every probability.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-HS: §3.2, PDF p.4, Eq.9 and following paragraph. The loss maximizes marginal probability of the selected set.

notes.text: In the soft version, the entire teacher distribution becomes the target through forward KL divergence.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-HS: §3.3, PDF p.4, opening paragraph and Eq.12, forward KL from teacher probabilities to student probabilities.

notes.text: These three bars are a teaching example, not benchmark measurements.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: original toy-probability example recorded in the source ledger; no experimental provenance is asserted.

notes.text: With teacher probabilities point six, point three and point one, an example threshold of point eight selects the first two documents.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: toy teacher [.6,.3,.1] and illustrative nucleus threshold .8; cumulative sum .9 selects A and B. The paper default threshold is different.

notes.text: Soft guidance retains the preference for the first document over the second, which the hard membership decision discards.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-HS: §3.3 opening paragraph explains that hard labels use teacher scores for a membership decision. DERIVATION: the A/B comparison applies that explanation to the toy example.

notes.text: In both cases, pseudo labels may be wrong, and the encoders remain unchanged.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.1 first and third paragraphs (frozen encoders and model-provided pseudo labels). Possibility of label error is a logical qualification.

pointers: Point to the bracket over A and B in Hard.
Then point to all three bar heights in Soft. The illustrative threshold is .8, not the paper default.
slides.caveat: Illustrative probabilities and threshold. TOUR Appendix D uses its own tuned settings.

slides.title:
Does moving the
query recover more?
slides.subtitle: TOUR paper · DPR on EntityQuestions · passage retrieval.
slides.takeaway: Reranking changes order; another search can change the set.

notes.text: This chart redraws TOUR Table three for the DPR passage retriever on EntityQuestions.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: PDF p.7, Table 3, DPR_multi rows and EntityQuestions columns.

notes.text: The vertical axis is answer-containing passage accuracy, shown at depths twenty and one hundred.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: Table 3 caption and §4.3 paragraph defining top-K accuracy as presence of an answer in the retrieved passages.

notes.text: First compare retrieval with reranking: accuracy at twenty rises from 57.9 to 64.4, while accuracy at one hundred stays at 70.8.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: Table 3, EntityQuestions, DPR_multi and +Re-ranker rows: 57.9/70.8 and 64.4/70.8.

notes.text: The unchanged deeper value illustrates the fixed-candidate limitation discussed earlier.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: unchanged70.8 in Table 3. REFIT-I: fixed-set Recall@K premise. This is our interpretation of the table.

notes.text: Now follow the blue TOUR-soft bars: the reported values are 66.2 at twenty and 72.5 at one hundred.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: Table 3, EntityQuestions, DPR_multi +TOURsoft row: 66.2/72.5.

notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: Table 3 and §4.3 results paragraph. Interprets higher hit-rate after retrieval; it does not establish exact per-document identities.

notes.text: These are published results for a specific model and dataset, not our project measurements.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: Table 3 caption, dataset and model labels. These values are from the paper, not our run.

notes.text: They show the mechanism can help, without guaranteeing the same gain on another corpus.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-R: bounded interpretation of Table 3; no universal generalization claim.

slides.title:
Can we reuse
one scored set?
slides.subtitle: ReFIT performs many inexpensive vector updates before re-retrieval.
slides.takeaway: One teacher pass. Many vector steps. One fresh search.

notes.text: ReFIT starts from retrieve-and-rerank, separating an expensive feedback round from inexpensive optimization steps.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: Algorithm 1 and §3.2 final two paragraphs, PDF p.3; §5.4 contrasts inner update allocation with TOUR.

notes.text: The teacher scores a fixed candidate set once, and those scores remain targets throughout the inner update.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: Algorithm 1 computes teacher distribution once in step2, before the repeated query-vector update loop.

notes.text: The method performs one hundred query-vector steps in the reported main configuration, then runs a second retrieval over the corpus.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §4.1, PDF p.3, final sentence specifies n100; §3.2 final paragraph specifies second full-index retrieval.

notes.text: One hundred vector steps therefore does not mean one hundred calls to the reranker.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: Algorithm 1, step2 versus steps3–7. Counts gradient updates separately from teacher scoring.

notes.text: The objective makes the retriever distribution resemble the teacher distribution, while all model weights and document vectors remain fixed.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §3.2, Eqs.5–7, Algorithm 1; cached document embeddings are read from the index rather than updated.

notes.text: The paper normalizes both score lists separately and uses a teacher temperature of two.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §4.1, PDF p.3, first paragraph: separate min-max normalization and teacher temperature T2.

notes.text: Faithful reproduction matters because these details can change the optimization signal.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §4.1 normalization and temperature choices. Our implementation reasoning: these choices affect the distributions defining the loss.

notes.text: The contrast with TOUR is the organization of feedback and updates; both methods can retrieve new documents.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.2 step-and-retrieve paragraph. REFIT-M: Algorithm 1 and §3.2 final paragraph. Our comparison of the two update organizations.

pointers: Circle “score once”, then point inside the 100-step update box.
Follow the final arrow to the same full corpus index.

slides.title:
What is KL
teaching the student?
slides.subtitle: Minimize disagreement with a fixed teacher distribution.
slides.takeaway: Give more student probability to documents the teacher prefers.

notes.text: Teacher and student are distributions over the same candidates, not models we train together here.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §3.2 Eqs.5–7 and Algorithm 1; teacher scores fixed while query vector changes.

notes.text: The teacher distribution comes from reranker scores; the student distribution comes from the current query-document similarities.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §3.2 Eq.5 (reranker distribution) and Eq.6 (retriever distribution).

notes.text: Read the equation as a weighted penalty for disagreement, with teacher probabilities providing weights.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §3.2 Eq.7. Our reading of the standard forward-KL expression, expanded in the source ledger.

notes.text: We minimize KL from teacher to student; we do not maximize KL and we do not change the teacher.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-M: §3.2 Eq.7 and Algorithm 1 gradient-descent update. Direction is teacher to student.

notes.text: For a fixed teacher, this is equivalent to maximizing teacher-weighted log probability under the student.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: Source ledger, Forward KL, fixed teacher. The teacher-entropy term is constant with respect to the student vector.

notes.text: In the illustrative bars, the teacher favors document A while the student places too much probability on C.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: original toy distributions teacher[.6,.3,.1] and student[.2,.3,.5].

notes.text: A useful vector update should reduce that discrepancy, though the shared embedding geometry couples the candidate scores.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: one vector determines all candidate dot products, so candidate logits cannot generally be set independently.

notes.text: The distribution on the right illustrates closer agreement, not a guaranteed result of one gradient step.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: original closer distribution[.5,.3,.2], intentionally not claimed as a simulated optimizer iterate.

pointers: Read teacher first in KL(teacher ∥ student).
Point to A, then C, and use the “After” button to reveal an illustrative closer distribution.

Is the feedback
worth another search?
slides.subtitle: ReFIT paper · BEIR Recall@100 · Table 6.
slides.takeaway: Quality and total cost both belong in the comparison.

notes.exactLocation: REFIT-R: PDF p.6, Table 6, BEIR column, all five rows.

notes.text: Recall at one hundred rises from 66.8 for retrieval to 67.6 for the larger-pool reranking comparator.
notes.exactLocation: REFIT-R: Table 6 BEIR Retrieve66.8 and Rerank67.6. REFIT-M: §4.2 defines the rerank125 comparator.

slides.title:
Can one query
teach the next?
slides.subtitle: TTT-Embed changes how long feedback survives.
slides.takeaway: From a query-private update to a reusable external state.

notes.text: The previous methods adapt the representation of the query currently being served.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.1 instance-level query optimization. REFIT-M: §3.2 query-specific distillation.

notes.text: TTT-Embed asks whether some of that feedback can survive and help later queries without entering the encoder weights.

notes.text: Its related-work section describes TOUR as query-level optimization and ReFIT as distillation into a query vector before another search.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-RW: Appendix §8, PDF p.13, pseudo-relevance-feedback/query-adaptation paragraph, TOUR and ReFIT descriptions.

notes.text: The authors group these approaches as keeping the optimized state private to the current query.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-RW: same Appendix §8 paragraph, concluding query-private-state characterization.

notes.text: Point to the two paths: a private state is used once, while a shared residual can be reused by other queries.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 three scope definitions. The diagram is an original schematic of the stated reuse relationship.

notes.text: This is the TTT-Embed authors’ framing of prior work, not our experimental result.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-RW: Appendix §8 characterization is attributed to TTT-Embed; not an experiment by this project.

notes.text: The new organizing question is where the state should be shared when relevance judgments have a limited budget.

slides.title:
Three scopes.
One residual idea.
slides.subtitle: Global, task and query are sharing scopes—not three separate retrieval tasks.
slides.takeaway: The scope chooses who contributes feedback and who can reuse it.

notes.text: TTT-Embed defines three sharing scopes for an external residual.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3, PDF p.4, three sharing-scope definitions.

notes.text: A global vector pools feedback across tasks for one embedding model and serves every query using that model.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 global-wise definition.

notes.text: A task vector pools feedback only within a particular task and serves other queries from that task.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 task-wise definition.

notes.text: A query vector uses one query’s scored candidates and remains specific to that query.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 query-wise definition.

notes.text: The learning mechanism stays the same; the grouping of feedback and reuse changes.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 opening and following paragraphs: one objective with different feedback grouping and reuse.

notes.text: Global learning balances task contributions so tasks with more queries do not automatically dominate the loss.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: Appendix §10, PDF p.14, Eq.14 and explanation of task-balanced global weights.

notes.text: A query without its own feedback has no query-specific correction, but it can still receive a learned task or global correction.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 paragraph following the definitions, behavior for unrewarded queries.

notes.text: The tradeoff is sharing scarce feedback broadly or spending enough to specialize narrowly; the best choice is empirical.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 scope discussion. TTT-B: §4.1 empirical budget/scope comparison. The tradeoff is our synthesis of those statements.

pointers: Point to one shared vector on the left, one per task in the middle, one per query on the right.
Say “scope” every time; do not call the three columns tasks.

slides.title:
How does the
residual learn?
slides.subtitle: The residual is optimized outside the frozen embedding model.
slides.takeaway: Fit the teacher distribution, then control the correction magnitude.

notes.text: The student adds a learned residual to the original normalized query vector, then normalizes again.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-M: §2.2 Eq.3, normalized x_q+v used during learning.

notes.text: Its candidate probabilities are compared with fixed teacher probabilities through forward KL divergence.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-M: §2.2 Eq.2 teacher distribution, Eq.3 student distribution and Eq.4 forward-KL objective.

notes.text: The loss averages over the state’s feedback queries and adds a ridge penalty to discourage an excessive residual.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-M: §2.2 Eq.4. TTT-S: Appendix §10 query weights; the average can be task-balanced.

notes.text: Only the external residual is optimized; the embedding model, teacher and stored document vectors remain frozen.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-I: Figure 1 caption and §2 opening paragraph. TTT-M: Eq.4 optimizes only v.

notes.text: After learning, deployment scales the residual by alpha: n divided by n plus one.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-M: §2.4 Eq.5 and adjacent deployment paragraph; shrinkage is applied after the full-residual fit.

notes.text: Here n counts distinct rewarded queries, not documents, so one query scored against many documents still gives alpha equal to one half.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-M: §2.4 final paragraph defines n as distinct rewarded queries and gives query-wise alpha1/2.

notes.text: Shared states supported by more queries receive less shrinkage under this rule.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-M: §2.4 Eq.5; n/(n+1) increases toward1 as distinct rewarded-query count increases.

notes.text: The corrected vector searches the existing full index, so the result set can differ from the feedback candidates.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-P: Appendix §12, Embedding and retrieval protocol paragraph, full-corpus re-search using the corrected query.

pointers: Point to the blue v in the update formula; then the KL fitting term and ridge term.
Finish on n = rewarded queries and α = .5 for a query-private state.

slides.title:
What if the next document
adds missing evidence?
slides.subtitle: DISCo motivates collective query coverage.
slides.takeaway: Useful complementarity is coverage of the query.

notes.text: DISCo studies a different retrieval goal: selecting a small collection whose members collectively cover the query.
notes.exactLocation: DISCO: Abstract and §1 first two paragraphs; §2 formalizes collection-level query coverage.

notes.text: Its representations use contextual token or atom vectors, rather than requiring literal bigram or n-gram matches.
notes.exactLocation: DISCO: §2 notation paragraph, PDF pp.2–3, contextual atoms/token-vector representations. Literal n-gram matching is not a required mechanism.

notes.text: The illustrative matrix shows how four candidates cover three query facets.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: original four-document, three-facet coverage matrix in the source ledger; illustrative rather than measured.

notes.text: After choosing document one, document two adds almost the same coverage, while document four contributes strongly to a missing facet.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: toy matrix, conditional on d1 already selected; d2 marginal coverage.05 versus d4.80.

notes.text: The max-per-facet objective avoids giving repeated credit merely for covering an already covered component.
notes.exactLocation: DISCO: §3.1 Eq.2 and immediately following paragraph explaining max coverage of each query atom.

notes.text: This is query-focused complementarity; the paper does not explicitly optimize a generic diversity objective.
notes.exactLocation: DISCO: Appendix B, p.19, Diversity paragraph; Appendix E.5, p.23, final paragraph on not explicitly incorporating diversity.

notes.text: Full DISCo uses a specialized index; borrowing its objective on a candidate pool gives only a coverage-inspired selector.
notes.exactLocation: DISCO: §§3.3–3.4 augmented representation and specialized index. HYPOTHESIS: the restricted candidate-pool selector is our proposal, not the full DISCo algorithm.

notes.text: Our next question is whether choosing feedback candidates this way can improve a residual, which DISCo itself does not establish.
notes.exactLocation: HYPOTHESIS: proposed coverage-to-residual experiment; DISCo reports coverage retrieval, not this residual-learning combination.

pointers: Click d₂, then d₄ in the matrix to compare marginal coverage.
Point to facet C when explaining the .80 gain. All matrix values are illustrative.

slides.title:
Could better candidates
teach a better direction?
slides.subtitle: Our proposed bridge from collective coverage to residual learning.
slides.takeaway: Change the feedback set, then measure what the learned vector does.

notes.text: In a simplified softmax model, the gradient is a weighted sum of scored document vectors.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: Source ledger, Simplified gradient. Assumes unnormalized dot-product logits and fixed teacher probabilities.

notes.text: The weight for each document is the student probability minus the teacher probability.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: derivative of forward KL with respect to each student logit is p_student−p_teacher.

notes.text: This shows why the selected candidates matter: they determine the available directions in that local learning signal.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: chain rule yields a linear combination of selected document vectors; geometric interpretation is ours.

notes.text: If many candidates contribute similar directions, complementary evidence might expose useful disagreements that the initial neighborhood misses.
notes.exactLocation: HYPOTHESIS: proposed usefulness of complementary candidate directions; not an established result.

notes.text: It might also introduce irrelevant or noisy feedback, so the geometric picture is motivation rather than a proof of improvement.
notes.exactLocation: HYPOTHESIS: noise/irrelevance is a possibility considered by our proposal, not a measured failure rate.

notes.text: This simplified gradient omits the score and vector normalizations used by the actual methods.
notes.exactLocation: DERIVATION: displayed gradient omits ReFIT min-max score normalization and TTT-Embed unit normalization; it is not their exact implemented derivative.

notes.text: Generic complementary-retriever guidance already appears in GQR, and ReFIT already discusses informative negatives.
notes.exactLocation: GQR: abstract, complementary-retriever scores guiding a primary query embedding. REFIT-L: §6.6.1 on informative negatives.

notes.text: Our proposed contribution must therefore be the controlled coverage-based candidate selection study under a matched feedback budget.
notes.exactLocation: HYPOTHESIS: narrowed proposed contribution after the cited prior-art boundary; not an exhaustive novelty claim.

pointers: Compare the nearly aligned candidate arrows with the broader useful directions.
Point to “simplified” before explaining the gradient; end on the hypothesis label.

slides.title:
What would a
fair test look like?
slides.subtitle: Reduce the query sample; keep the complete document index.
slides.takeaway: Same teacher budget. Same residual learner. Different candidate selection.

notes.text: Begin with one hundred to two hundred prespecified queries, retaining the full document corpus.
notes.exactLocation: DESIGN: proposed query sampling protocol requested by the user; full corpus retained in every arm.

notes.text: Fewer queries reduce cost but cannot guarantee the paper’s average or a narrow uncertainty interval.
notes.exactLocation: DESIGN: statistical qualification: sample size alone does not determine the mean or confidence-interval width.

notes.text: Compare base top-K feedback with a coverage-inspired selector, plus a broader-pool control and random selection from the same pool.
notes.exactLocation: DESIGN: proposed candidate-selection controls, not previously completed runs.

notes.text: Fix query identifiers, teacher, student embeddings, feedback count, loss, optimizer and sharing scope across candidate selectors.
notes.exactLocation: PLAN: controlled-comparison design, acquisition-policy comparison. DESIGN: hold the learner and budget fixed while candidate identities may differ.

notes.text: Charge additional retrieval and selection separately, even if teacher-pair counts match.
notes.exactLocation: DESIGN: cost-accounting proposal; equal teacher counts do not imply equal full runtime.

notes.text: Search the full index after adaptation, then report nDCG, recall, paired uncertainty and judged positives found outside the initial pool.
notes.exactLocation: DESIGN: proposed full-index evaluation, paired estimates and judged-positive discovery measures.

notes.text: For shared states, separate feedback queries from held-out evaluation queries; report single-query adaptation as a different regime.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-P: §4.2 and Table 2 distinguish held-out-query transfer. DESIGN: our proposed separation of feedback and evaluation queries.

notes.text: Any helper retriever supplies document IDs; the residual still uses vectors from the same frozen student embedding space.
notes.exactLocation: DESIGN: implementation consequence of using a single frozen student embedding space; helper-vector dimensions cannot be substituted into that objective.

pointers: Point to the full-corpus block: it stays intact in every arm.
Trace selector A and B into the identical learner, then the same evaluation.

slides.title:
What can we
conclude today?
slides.subtitle: A testable direction, with clear evidence boundaries.
slides.takeaway: Can coverage-aware feedback make each judgment more useful?

notes.text: The literature shows that relevance scores can improve query representations without updating model weights.
notes.exactLocation: TOUR-M: §3.1–3.3 frozen encoders and optimized query vector. REFIT-M: §3.2 same output-space adaptation principle.

notes.text: TTT-Embed studies persistent external states and how sharing scope interacts with the feedback budget.
notes.exactLocation: TTT-S: §2.3 scope definitions. TTT-B: §4.1/Table 1 budget-dependent empirical comparison.

notes.text: Our SCIDOCS attempt matches the raw and reranking references, but leaves the ReFIT adaptation gain unresolved.
notes.exactLocation: RUN: three SCIDOCS measured values. REFIT-SCI: v2 Table 2 references; matching means at displayed precision.

notes.text: Next, we propose examining which documents supply the learning signal, rather than assuming a different update rule is enough.
notes.exactLocation: HYPOTHESIS: proposed candidate-selection focus, not a causal explanation of the reproduction gap.

notes.text: DISCo offers a coverage principle that may guide selection, while GQR and earlier feedback work constrain what we can claim as new.
notes.exactLocation: DISCO: §3.1 coverage objective. GQR: abstract complementary guidance. REFIT-L: §6.6.1 informative negatives. Our synthesis defines a narrower question.

notes.text: We will call the combination useful only if a controlled comparison improves retrieval under disclosed feedback and computation costs.
notes.exactLocation: DESIGN: prospective success criterion, requiring a controlled measured gain and disclosed costs.

notes.text: The FiQA pilot reports no reliable held-out gain, while coverage-aware selection still awaits a controlled test.
notes.exactLocation: FIQA_RUN: §4 table, FiQA Interpretation column reports no reliable held-out transfer; paragraph immediately after the table says neither completed measurement tests complementary selection. HYPOTHESIS: the controlled selection comparison remains proposed.

notes.text: The next experiment is designed to answer that question.
